summary: Describes a Uniform Resource Name namespace convention for the New Zealand Government. It is used to identify, name, assign, and manage persistent resources and XML artefacts. The document is informational.

eli5.summary: Permanent name tags for government documents, so something can always be found by its name even if its address changes.

questions: what is the nzl urn namespace
how are new zealand government documents named
subtitle: A persistent naming standard for New Zealand Government documents and data.

tldr.problem: The New Zealand Government publishes XML documents and schemas but needs globally unique, persistent identifiers that do not depend on where files are stored.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers a URN namespace identifier (NID) called 'NZL' (the ISO 3166 Alpha-3 country code) with a hierarchical structure starting with a 'govt' specifier managed by the State Services Commission.
tldr.outcome: Government agencies can create permanent names following the NZGLS (New Zealand Government Locator Service) thesaurus, making it easier to identify and reference documents even if their location changes.

facts.label: Basis for terms
facts.value: NZGLS (New Zealand Government Locator Service) thesaurus

today: RFC 4350 is an Informational RFC that defines the NZL URN namespace for the New Zealand Government. The namespace has been registered with IANA and provides a framework for government agencies and organizations to create persistent, unique identifiers for their documents and data structures.

sections.title: Why Government Needs Persistent Names
sections.content:
When a government publishes documents, schemas, and XML artifacts (structured data), it needs a way to name them that does not change even if the document moves to a different web server. A Uniform Resource Name (URN) is a persistent identifier that is separate from a location.

The New Zealand Government had already adopted XML as its primary means of storing and exchanging data. To avoid agencies creating conflicting naming structures, the government wanted a unified naming convention, especially for the Dublin Core-based metadata standard called the NZGLS (New Zealand Government Locator Service), which government agencies use to describe their resources.

This RFC registers the URN namespace identifier (NID) 'NZL' for New Zealand Government resources, with a hierarchical structure that allows multiple agencies to create names under a common framework.
sections.eli5: Government documents move around on the internet, but they should have permanent names that stay the same no matter where they are stored. This is like a person's social security number, which identifies them no matter where they move.

sections.title: The URN Structure
sections.content:
The NZL URN has a hierarchical format:

urn:nzl:<nz-specifier>[:<nz-specifier-defined-string>]+

The first part after 'nzl' is a specifier, which identifies a category or organization. The government manages the 'govt' specifier, which is further divided using terms from the NZGLS thesaurus. For example:

  • urn:nzl:govt:registering:dogs:registration:1-0
  • urn:nzl:govt:registering:firearms:form:1-3

Each component separated by a colon (except the first colon, which is a delimiter) is an nz-specifier-defined string. All components must be UTF-8 characters compliant with URI syntax and cannot contain colons themselves.

The State Services Commission (SSC) manages the 'govt' specifier and can assign other specifiers (like 'mil' for military, 'co' for commercial, 'org' for organizations) to other entities that apply and demonstrate they can manage their sub-levels responsibly.
sections.eli5: The name is like an address book entry: 'New Zealand / Government / Registering / Dogs / Registration / Version 1-0'. Colons separate the levels, and each agency can manage their own sub-levels under the government framework.

sections.title: Who Manages the Namespace
sections.content:
The State Services Commission (SSC) is the registered entity responsible for the NZL namespace. The SSC has extensive experience managing similar structures: since 2002 it has maintained the NZGLS thesaurus, and it has moderated the .govt.nz top-level domain for websites.

For the 'govt' specifier, the SSC ensures that all assigned URNs are unique by checking against a registry of previously assigned names. When other organizations apply to manage their own specifiers (like 'mil' or 'co'), the SSC requires them to follow robust processes for resolution and management.

The assignment process is transparent: the SSC publishes lists of assigned identifiers on its web pages at http://www.e.govt.nz/, and follows policies similar to those used for the .govt.nz domain (published in moderation policies). This prevents squatting or hoarding of names.
sections.eli5: One government office (the State Services Commission) keeps the master list and makes sure no two things get the same name. They follow rules like those for .govt.nz domain names, which are fair and public.

sections.title: Scope and Community
sections.content:
While the namespace is global in scope (URNs are resolved on the internet), it is primarily of national interest to New Zealand. The government intends that both public agencies and private sector organizations in New Zealand can use it for data exchange.

The benefits extend beyond government: providers of government information gain guidance on generating target namespaces for XML schema development using a process they already understand (the NZGLS). Citizens and organizations with internet access can view the namespace and its associated registration and resolution services.

The RFC acknowledges a unique feature: this is the first known use of an ISO 3166 Alpha-3 country code as a URN NID. The code NZL is globally known and ensures uniqueness.
sections.eli5: This naming system is available to anyone in New Zealand for identifying documents, and it helps organizations structure their data in a way that others can easily understand and access.

sections.title: Handling Accents and Language
sections.content:
The RFC addresses a special consideration: Maori, one of New Zealand's official languages, uses diacritical marks (macrons over vowels), and these marks can change word meaning. For example, 'Maori' with a macron is written as M%C4%81ori when percent-encoded in URIs.

The NZGLS thesaurus does not currently use diacritical marks, so the 'govt' specifier will not need to use them either. There is no mapping or equivalence: 'Maori' without a macron is simply written as 'maori'.

However, other organizations managing their own specifiers may use UTF-8's diacritical functionality if they have processes to distinguish between terms with macrons and those without, ensuring they remain unique.

For lexical equivalence, URN names are compared case-insensitively, so 'GOVT' and 'govt' are treated as the same. This prevents two different names from differing only by case.
sections.eli5: Government documents are written in both English and Maori. The naming system carefully handles Maori spelling so that similar-looking names are not confused with each other, and the system is case-insensitive (uppercase and lowercase are treated the same).
